lessons.title: Residential vs Commercial Yields: Why Offices and Warehouses Pay More

children.text: Navi Mumbai, same budget, two brochures. A 3BHK in Kharghar for ₹1.5 crore rents for ₹38,000 a month, about 3% gross. A pre-leased office unit in Vashi for the same ₹1.5 crore rents for ₹90,000 a month, 7.2% gross. The office pays more than twice the rent on the same money. So why do most Indian investors still buy flats? Because that extra yield is not a gift. It is the market paying you to carry risks a flat owner rarely faces. By the end of this lesson you will know where offices, warehouses and shops sit on the yield ladder, the six reasons they pay more, and how to tell whether the extra yield is worth what it asks of you.

body.text: A higher yield is never free. Commercial property pays more because it asks you to accept longer vacancies, a single tenant, bigger tickets, fewer buyers and slower appreciation.

Three Ways to Invest ₹1.5 Crore

Using the same gross-to-net method from the last lesson, here are three illustrative ₹1.5 crore options around Mumbai. The office tenant pays common area maintenance while in occupation, and so does the warehouse tenant, but each owner bears property tax, insurance, brokerage and costs during vacancy.

children.text: The office loses a bigger share of its rent to leakage (27%) than the flat (21%), mainly because vacancy is longer and brokerage is larger. Even so, its net yield is still more than double the flat's. The question is not whether commercial property pays more on paper. It clearly does. The question is what you are giving up to get it.
Six Reasons Commercial Property Pays More
No emotional buyers.

Flats are bought by families who want to live in them, and that demand pushes prices above what rent alone would justify. Nobody moves into a warehouse. Commercial property is priced almost entirely on the income it produces, much like a bond.
Vacancy is long and lumpy.
A 2BHK in a busy suburb can find a tenant in weeks. An office unit or warehouse can sit empty for many months, sometimes more than a year, while you keep paying property tax and maintenance.
One tenant is all your income.
A company that downsizes, relocates to a newer building or shuts down takes 100% of your rent with it. This concentration risk is why tenant quality matters so much more in commercial property.
Buildings go out of date.

Office tenants increasingly want large floor plates, green certification and full power backup. Logistics tenants want high clear heights, loading docks and highway access. An older building can lose tenants to a newer one down the road, however well it is maintained.
Bigger tickets, fewer buyers.

Thousands of families can buy a ₹1.5 crore flat. Far fewer investors want a ₹1.5 crore office unit, and fewer still a warehouse. When you need to sell, a thinner pool of buyers means a longer wait or a lower price.
Appreciation mostly follows rent.

Because commercial property is priced on income, its value tends to rise when rents rise, not because of hope. That makes the growth engine steadier but usually slower, so more of the total return has to come from yield.

body.title: Spot the odd one out
body.question: Which of these is NOT a reason commercial property is priced at a higher yield than residential flats?
options: Vacancies between tenants tend to last much longer
A single tenant usually provides all of the income
Commercial tenants often sign longer leases with lock-in periods
Far fewer buyers can afford or want commercial units
body.explanation: Longer leases with lock-ins reduce risk, because they lock in income for years. If anything, they support a lower yield. The other three options all add risk, which is why buyers demand a higher yield to take them on.

cells: Several months to a year or more

body.text: A 15% escalation every three years works out to about 4.8% a year compounded, similar to a residential renewal. The real difference is certainty. A commercial escalation is written into a multi-year lease. A residential increase has to be renegotiated every 11 months, and the tenant can simply leave.

children.text: The Bad Year Test

Average net yields hide how income behaves when things go wrong. Compare a bad year for each property: the flat sits empty for three months, while the office and the warehouse each lose their tenant and stay empty for the full year, then pay brokerage to re-let.

body.title: Net Income in a Bad Year (₹ lakh)
Show me the math: the bad year

children.text: Kharghar flat:

rent for 9 months = ₹3,42,000. Costs = brokerage ₹38,000 + property tax ₹10,000 + repairs ₹15,000 + sinking fund ₹6,000 + maintenance while empty ₹13,500 + insurance ₹3,000 + agreement and verification ₹2,000 = ₹87,500. Net income = ₹2,54,500.
Vashi office:

rent = zero. Costs = CAM while empty ₹12,000 × 12 = ₹1,44,000 + property tax ₹40,000 + insurance ₹5,000 + brokerage of two months' rent ₹1,80,000 + refurbishment for the next tenant ₹60,000 = ₹4,29,000. Net income = − ₹4,29,000.
Bhiwandi warehouse:
rent = zero. Costs = property tax ₹30,000 + insurance ₹10,000 + repairs ₹40,000 + brokerage of two months' rent ₹2,20,000 = ₹3,00,000. Net income = − ₹3,00,000.

body.label: Swing from a normal year to a bad year, Vashi office
body.context: From ₹7.86 lakh of net income to a loss of ₹4.29 lakh. One empty year wipes out roughly a year and a half of normal net income.

children.text: Price Is Rent Divided by Yield

markDefs.definition: A property sold with a tenant already in place and paying rent, usually marketed on its rental yield.

children.text: Because commercial property is priced on income, a
pre-leased

unit's price is simply its rent divided by the yield buyers demand. That creates a risk flat owners feel less directly: if buyers start demanding a higher yield, the price falls even when the rent has not changed at all. Chapter 4 develops this idea as the cap rate.

body.title: When buyers want more yield
body.prompt: The Vashi office still earns ₹10,80,000 a year in rent. After a rise in interest rates, buyers of similar units now demand an 8% gross yield instead of 7.2%. What would the office sell for now, in crore? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Price = ₹10,80,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₹1,35,00,000, or ₹1.35 crore. The rent did not change, but the value fell by ₹15 lakh, or 10%, only because buyers now want a higher yield.

body.title: Name the pitch
body.textWithBlank: A shop sold with a bank already paying rent in it is marketed as a ___ property.
body.explanation: Pre-leased properties are sold on the strength of their existing tenant and rent. The tenant is the main thing you are buying, so check the lease as carefully as the building.

body.text: Be very careful with "assured rental" or "lease guarantee" schemes where the developer, not a real tenant, promises you a fixed yield for a few years. The payments often stop when the guarantee period ends or the developer runs short of cash, and the unit may have no genuine tenant behind it. A real pre-leased property has a registered lease with an identifiable, creditworthy tenant.

body.title: The pre-leased bank branch
body.scenario: Harpreet Kaur, a 48-year-old business owner in Ludhiana, is offered a ground-floor shop on Ferozepur Road for ₹2 crore, leased to a private sector bank at ₹1,25,000 a month. The nine-year lease started four years ago, the three-year lock-in has already ended, and the next 15% escalation is due in two years. The seller says: "7.5% yield from a bank. Safer than any flat."
body.prompt: Check the seller's yield, then list the risks and the questions Harpreet should ask before buying.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Gross yield: ₹1,25,000 × 12 = ₹15,00,000. ₹15,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,00,000 × 100 = 7.5%. The arithmetic is right, but it is gross, on agreement value, before stamp duty and costs.
2. The lock-in is over. The bank can now exit with the notice period in the lease. Banks do consolidate branches, especially after mergers or when customers move to digital banking, so a strong tenant is not the same as a guaranteed one.
3. Five years remain on the lease. The yield is only as secure as the bank's willingness to stay, and the lease must be read for exit clauses, notice periods and renewal terms.
4. Is the rent above market? If similar shops on Ferozepur Road rent for ₹1,00,000, a new tenant would pay less, and the yield on ₹2 crore would drop to 6%.
5. If buyers of similar shops later demand 8.5% instead of 7.5%, the same ₹15 lakh rent supports a price of only about ₹1.76 crore, roughly 12% less.
6. Single-tenant risk: if the bank leaves, income falls to zero while property tax and maintenance continue, and a ground-floor bank space may need changes to suit a new retailer.
7. Questions to ask: a copy of the registered lease deed; the bank's exit and notice clauses; rent paid by comparable shops nearby; how long similar units have stayed vacant; property tax and any society or market association charges; and GST registration requirements on commercial rent.

columns.label: Commercial property may suit you if
points: You need higher income today rather than growth
You can absorb a year or more with zero rent
You can judge tenant quality and read a lease deed
You will not need to sell quickly
Your ticket size does not concentrate most of your wealth in one unit

columns.label: A residential flat may suit you better if
points: You want a large pool of tenants and buyers
A long empty period would strain your finances
You may live in the property yourself one day
You are comfortable relying more on appreciation
You prefer simple, standard rent agreements

children.text: There is a third route. Listed REITs such as Embassy Office Parks, Mindspace Business Parks, Brookfield India REIT and Nexus Select Trust let you own a slice of hundreds of commercial tenants for the price of a few units on NSE or BSE, which spreads out single-tenant and vacancy risk. We cover them in Chapter 5.

A property sold with a paying tenant already in place, usually marketed on its yield.
The minimum lease period during which neither side can exit without paying the remaining rent.
A lease term that raises rent by a set percentage at fixed intervals.
Common area maintenance costs in commercial buildings, usually paid by the tenant while in occupation.
Commercial property value falls when buyers demand a higher yield, even if the rent is unchanged.
A developer's promise of fixed returns for a period. It is not the same as a lease with a real tenant.

points: Indicative gross yields rise from about 2% to 4% for flats to about 6% to 8% for strata offices and about 7% to 9% for warehouses.
On ₹1.5 crore, a Kharghar flat nets about 2.4%, a Vashi office about 5.2% and a Bhiwandi warehouse about 7.0% in this illustration.
The extra yield pays for real risks: no owner-occupier demand, long vacancies, single-tenant concentration, obsolescence, fewer buyers and slower appreciation.
Commercial leases offer lock-ins, written escalations and tenant-paid CAM, which make income more predictable while the tenant stays.
In a bad year, a flat still earns something, but a vacant office or warehouse can lose money.
Commercial prices equal rent divided by the yield buyers demand, so values can fall even when rent is unchanged.
Treat developer-assured rental schemes with great caution; a real tenant on a registered lease is what you are paying for.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice, and the REITs named are not recommendations. The people, properties, rents, yields, vacancy periods and costs shown are illustrative. Commercial lease terms vary widely by deal and city, so read the actual lease deed and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a property lawyer before making any decision.
